client: Hey Luna, I've been really stressed out lately. I just started this new job at a tech startup, and I feel like I'm constantly falling behind on my project deadlines. It's overwhelming, and I'm not sure if I can keep up. I know I should be grateful for the opportunity, but it's hard not to feel like I’m drowning.
therapist: It sounds like you're really feeling the pressure of your new role, and it’s completely understandable to feel overwhelmed with all the new responsibilities. The fast pace and high expectations can be a lot to handle. How are you coping with these feelings, and have you found any moments of relief or support that might help you navigate this challenging time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Thanks for understanding, Luna. I've been trying to stay on top of things by working long hours, but it’s really taking a toll on me. I haven’t really found much relief; I feel like I’m constantly on edge. I know I should reach out for support, but I’m worried about looking incompetent or like I can’t handle the job.
therapist: I can hear how much you’re struggling, and it’s completely natural to feel this way when you’re under so much pressure. It sounds like you’re really pushing yourself to the limit, and it’s taking a toll on your well-being. It’s important to remember that reaching out for support isn’t a sign of weakness; it’s a sign of strength and a way to ensure you can keep going. Have you thought about talking to a trusted colleague or your manager about how you’re feeling? They might be able to offer some support or adjustments that could help you feel less overwhelmed.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I appreciate your encouragement, Luna, but I’m really hesitant to talk to my manager or colleagues. I feel like they’ll think I’m not cut out for the job, and that could affect my position. It’s hard to open up when I’m already feeling so vulnerable and unsure.
therapist: I can hear the hesitation and vulnerability in your voice, and it’s completely understandable to feel that way. It’s natural to worry about how others might perceive you, especially when you’re already feeling unsure. Have you considered any small steps you could take to ease into seeking support, perhaps by reaching out to a mentor or someone you trust outside of your immediate team? Sometimes, just having a sounding board can make a big difference.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: You’re right, Luna. I do remember a time when I shared a work issue with a colleague, and they were really supportive and helped me find a solution. It didn’t go as badly as I feared. But this feels different somehow—bigger and more personal. I guess I’m still struggling with the idea of being vulnerable in a new and high-pressure environment.
therapist: It sounds like you’re in a challenging place, and it’s understandable that this new environment feels more intense and personal. I can hear a bit of a tension in your voice, like there’s a part of you that’s trying to balance the fear of vulnerability with the potential for support. client: I think part of it is the pressure to prove myself in this new role. I feel like I have a lot to lose if I show any weakness. It’s different from before because I’m starting from scratch and really want to make a good impression. I guess I’m just afraid that any sign of struggle will be seen as a lack of competence.
therapist: I can hear how much pressure you’re putting on yourself to prove your worth in this new role. It’s completely natural to want to make a strong impression, especially when you’re starting from scratch. The fear of showing any weakness can be really intense, and it’s clear that you’re carrying a lot of weight with this. Have you noticed any moments, no matter how small, where you’ve felt a sense of accomplishment or where you’ve received positive feedback? Sometimes, even the smallest successes can help build confidence and ease some of that pressure.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: You know, Luna, I did get some positive feedback on a project I completed last week. My team lead said I did a good job on the initial design phase. It felt good to hear that, but it was also a fleeting moment. I find it hard to hold onto those positive feelings when the workload and expectations are so high. It’s like every small win gets overshadowed by the next big challenge.
therapist: It’s really great that you’re able to acknowledge those moments of positive feedback, even if they feel fleeting. It sounds like you’re holding onto a lot of pressure, and it’s understandable that each new challenge can overshadow those small wins. It’s important to give yourself permission to recognize and celebrate those positive moments, no matter how brief they might seem. How do you think you could create more space to acknowledge and hold onto those good feelings, even as you face new challenges?
